parole.significato: abutilon; Indian mallow (any plant of the genus Abutilon)
parole.testo: From the genus name Abutilon, from Arabic أَبُو طِيلُون (ʔabū ṭīlūn). Doublet of botilhão and butilhão.

parole.significato: chard (Beta vulgaris, sometimes Beta vulgaris var. cicla)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic السِّلْقَة (as-silqa). Compare Galician, Fala, and Spanish acelga.

parole.significato: appetiser, antipasto, hors d'oeuvre (food served before the main course)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic اَلزَّبِيب (az-zabīb, “raisin”). Compare Spanish acebibe.
Uncertain origin, most probably from Arabic, either from شَكَّ (šakka, “to doubt”) or شَكَا (šakā, “to complain”). Cognate with Spanish achaque, Galician achaque and Catalan xacra.
Borrowed from Arabic السِّقَاط (as-siqāṭ).
Derived from Arabic ستارة (“as-sitāra”)
Borrowed from Arabic الشَّحْم (“grease, fat”).

parole.significato: a type of oval or heart-shaped leather shield
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic دَرَقَة (daraqa, “shield”), via Andalusian Arabic.

parole.significato: thrift shop (shop which sells used goods)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الدَلَّال (ad-dallāl, “auctioneer”).

parole.significato: adhan (the call to prayer, usually recited by a muezzin before each of the five obligatory daily prayers)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic أَذَان (ʔaḏān).
Borrowed from Arabic اَلطُّوب (aṭ-ṭūb).

parole.significato: a traditional square tambourine of Moorish origin
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese adufe, from Arabic الدُّفّ (ad-duff, “tambourine”), from Middle Persian 𐭣𐭯 (dp /⁠dap⁠/, “daf”), from Sumerian 𒁾 (dub, “tablet”). Compare Galician adufe.
From a- + Arabic خَلَقَ (ḵalaqa) + -ar. Compare Spanish halagar.

parole.significato: a milk flock of sheep or of she-goats
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic لَبَن (laban), through Andalusian Arabic.
From alacrau, from Arabic العَقْرَب (al-ʕaqrab, “scorpion”), from the beetle's habit of lifting up its rear end when threatened.
From the noun alambique (“still”), from Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq, “still”), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix).

parole.significato: alembic (chemical apparatus used to purify substances by distillation)
parole.testo: From Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq, “still”), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup, cap of a still”). Compare English alembic, French alambic, Spanish alambique.
Borrowed from Arabic العَنْبَر (al-ʕanbar).
Perhaps onomatopoeic, related to alalá, or from Arabic عَرِيض (ʕarīḍ).
From Old Galician-Portuguese allarve, from Arabic العَرَب (al-ʕarab, “the Arabs”). Doublet of árabe.
Borrowed from Arabic أَصْهَب (ʔaṣhab, “reddish, reddish-brown”), via Andalusian Arabic.
Borrowed from Arabic الْعُود (al-ʕūd), via Andalusian Arabic. Compare Spanish laúd.
From Arabic البَرْدَعَة (al-bardaʕa), variant of البَرْذَعَة (al-barḏaʕa, “packsaddle”).

parole.significato: burnoose (a thick hooded cloak used in northern Africa)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic بُرْنُس (burnus, “burnoose”) via Andalusian Arabic, from Ancient Greek βίρρος (bírrhos).
Borrowed from Arabic الْبُحَيْرَة (al-buḥayra), via Andalusian Arabic. Doublet of almofeira.

parole.significato: green rye, wheat, barley, oats used as fodder
parole.testo: From Arabic قَصِيل (qaṣīl).

parole.significato: artichoke (an edible plant related to the thistle)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic اَلْخَرْشُوف (al-ḵaršūf, “artichoke”).

parole.significato: a small earthen ball filled with flowers, ashes and colourful strips thrown by horsemen at each other during jousts
parole.testo: Derived from Arabic كَنْز (kanz), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Spanish alcancía.
From Arabic الكَبَّار (al-kabbār).
Borrowed from Arabic الكَرَاوِيَا (al-karāwiyā).

From Arabic الكُرَّاز (al-kurrāz), from Aramaic כרז / כרוז (“a type of container”), possibly from Akkadian 𒆳𒍣𒍝𒆪 (/⁠kurziza, kurzizakku⁠/, “a basket, container”), from Sumerian 𒄥𒋛𒁲 (/⁠gursisa⁠/, “basket, container”, literally “normal or standard 𒄥 (gur)”).
Borrowed from Arabic الْقَطِيعَ (al-qaṭīʕa, “herd”).

parole.significato: carpet (a fabric used as a floor covering)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic القَطِيفَة (al-qaṭīfa). Compare Catalan catifa.

parole.significato: rump (cut of meat from the rump of an animal)
parole.testo: From Arabic القَطْرَة (al-qaṭra, “piece, drop”).

parole.significato: any of several species of seabird
parole.testo: Probably from Arabic الْغَطَّاس (al-ḡaṭṭās, “the diver”). Not derived from modern Arabic الْقَطْرَس (al-qaṭras, “the albatross”), which is instead perhaps borrowed from Spanish. Doublet of albatroz, a twice-borrowed term. Alternative theories include: from alcatruz (“well bucket”), referring to the

From Old Galician-Portuguese alcatruz (“noria bucket”), from Arabic الْقَادُوس (al-qādūs, “skep”), from Ancient Greek κάδος (kádos, “bucket”). Compare with Spanish arcaduz, Catalan caduf, and Sicilian catusu.

parole.significato: tar (resinous substance composed of liquid pitch, resin and oil or tallow)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic القَطْرَان (al-qaṭrān). Compare Spanish alquitrán.
Borrowed from Arabic عِرْق السُوس (ʕirq as-sūs, “liquorice root”), via Andalusian Arabic.
From Arabic القُفَّة (al-quffa).

parole.significato: a sweet from the Alentejo region, having a rhomboid shape, made from toasted wheat flour, honey or sugar, water and pin…
parole.testo: Ultimately from Arabic كَمُّون (kammūn, “cumin”).
From Arabic القُبَّة (al-qubba, “the vault, chamber with vaulted roof”).
Borrowed from Arabic الكُنْيَة (al-kunya, “surname”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese alcacer /alcaçar, from Arabic قَصْر (qaṣr), via Andalusian Arabic. Doublet of castro.

parole.significato: a Moorish fortress within or beside a walled city
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic قَصَبَة (qaṣaba), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Spanish alcazaba and English casbah. Doublet of casbá.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aldeia, aldea, from Arabic اَلضَّيْعَة (aḍ-ḍayʕa, “village”). Cognate with Galician, Asturian, and Spanish aldea, Mirandese aldé and Aragonese aldeya.
From Arabic الضَبَّة (aḍ-ḍabba, “window-bolt”, literally “lizard”). Compare Spanish aldaba.
Borrowed from Arabic اَلإِكْلِيل (al-ʔiklīl), ellipsis of إِكْلِيل الْجَبَل (ʔiklīl al-jabal, “rosemary”).

parole.significato: deceit (act or practice intended to deceive)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aleive, from Arabic العَيْب (al-ʕayb). Cognate with Spanish aleve.
Borrowed from Arabic الخَيْرِيّ (al-ḵayriyy). Cognate of Spanish alhelí.
Borrowed from Arabic الْإِطْرِيَة (al-ʔiṭriya) via Andalusian Arabic, from Aramaic אִטְרִיתָא (ʾiṭrīṯā), from Ancient Greek ἴτριον (ítrion). Compare Spanish aletría.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alfaça, from Arabic الْخَسّ (al-ḵass). First attested in c. 16th century. Cognate with Galician alfaza and Maltese ħass.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alfalfa, from Arabic الْفَصْفَصَة (al-faṣfaṣa).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alfaia, from Arabic الحَاجَة (al-ḥāja, “necessary thing; valuable thing”). Compare Galician alfaia and Spanish alhaja.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alfaiate, from Arabic الْخَيَّاط (al-ḵayyāṭ, “the tailor”). Compare Galician alfaiate.
From Arabic الحَاجِز (al-ḥājiz).

parole.significato: a small Andalusian horse used by Moorish cavalry
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الفرس (“al-farās”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese alfarroba, borrowed from Arabic خَرُّوب (ḵarrūb), borrowed from Aramaic חַרּוּבָא. Compare Spanish algarroba.
From Arabic الحَبَق (al-ḥabaq, “basil”).
From Arabic اَلْخُزَامَى (al-ḵuzāmā). Cognate with Spanish alhucema.
Borrowed from Arabic الحَيْر (al-ḥayr).
Borrowed from Arabic الفَارِس (al-fāris, “knight”), with sense influenced by Latin aquilifer (“standard-bearer”).
Borrowed from Arabic خِلَال (ḵilāl, “pin, peg”), via Andalusian Arabic.
Borrowed from Arabic الحُلْبَة (al-ḥulba).
Borrowed from Arabic خُرْج (ḵurj, “saddlebag”), via Andalusian Arabic. Compare Spanish alforja.
From Arabic الحُرَّيْقَة (al-ḥurrayqa, “the nettle”), via Andalusian Arabic. Compare Maltese ħurrieq.

parole.significato: manumission (act of a slave owner freeing his or her slaves)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic اَلْحُرِّيَّة (al-ḥurriyya, “the freedom”). Compare Spanish alhorría.
Borrowed from Arabic الْفُنْدُق (al-funduq, “inn”) via Andalusian Arabic, from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon, “inn”). Cognate to Spanish alhóndiga and Catalan alfòndec.
From Old Galician-Portuguese algaravia, from Arabic الْعَرَبِيَّة (al-ʕarabiyya, “Arabic [language]”), via Andalusian Arabic. Compare Galician and Spanish algarabía.
Borrowed from Arabic الغَزَارَة (al-ḡazāra, “abundance”). Compare Galician and Spanish algazara, Catalan gatzara and Italian gazzarra.
Borrowed from Arabic ألجام (“a shackle of iron”), the plural form of the noun لجم or لجام which also refers to a harness of a horse. It is derived from the root ل ج م.

parole.significato: gutter (duct or channel beneath the eaves)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic زُرُوب (zurūb), plural of زِرْب (zirb), via Andalusian Arabic.
From Arabic اَلْجُبّ (al-jubb, “the cistern, the well”), via Andalusian Arabic. Doublet of aljube.

parole.significato: person or store that sells clothing made from cheap fabric
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الْجِلْبَاب (al-jilbāb). First attested in the 16th century.
Borrowed from Arabic الغُزّ (al-ḡuzz, “Oghuz, a tribe of kafir Turkic mercenary”).
From Arabic اَلْوَزِير (al-wazīr, “minister, vizier”). Doublet of vizir.

parole.significato: an earthenware, plastic, or metal bowl in the form of an inverted, truncated cone
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic القدر (“large wooden bowl”).
Borrowed from Arabic لَقَّاط (laqqāṭ), via Andalusian Arabic.
Borrowed from Arabic الأَسَاس (al-ʔasās, “foundation”). Cognate with Galician alicerce.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aljava, borrowed from Arabic جَعْبَة (jaʕba). Cognate with Galician alxaba.
Borrowed from Arabic اَلْجُبّ (al-jubb, “the cistern, the well”). Doublet of algibe.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese aljoufar, from Arabic الجَوْهَر (al-jawhar, “jewel, pearl”), from Persian گوهر (gowhar, “jewel, pearl”), from Middle Persian gwhl (gōhr, “substance, essence; jewel”), from Old Persian *gauθra, *gavaθra, from Proto-Indo-European. Cognate with Galician alxofre an
From Arabic مَطْرَح (maṭraḥ, “place where something is thrown”). Cognate with English mattress.

parole.significato: a beam which connects an animal to a mill
parole.testo: From Arabic المَجَرَّة (al-majarra, “the beam”).

parole.significato: torch or bonfire lit at the top of a tower or high point to transmit signals visible from a distance
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الْمَنَارَة (al-manāra). Doublet of minarete.
Borrowed from Arabic الْمُكَارِي (al-mukārī⁩, “muleteer”).

parole.significato: a cemetery for Moors or Jews, during the 14th and 15th centuries
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic المقبرة (al-maqbara).
Borrowed from Arabic المُنَادَة (al-munāda). Cognate with Galician almoeda and Spanish almoneda.
Ultimately from Arabic الْمُرَابِط (al-murābiṭ). Doublet of marabuto.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese almetolia, from Arabic المُطْلِيَة (al-muṭliya).
Borrowed from Arabic المُشْرِف (al-mušrif).
Borrowed from Arabic المَأْذَنة (al-maʔḏana).
From Arabic مُصْطَكَى (muṣṭakā), ultimately from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē).
Borrowed from Arabic المِسْك (al-misk) via Andalusian Arabic, from Persian مشک (mošk), from Sanskrit मुष्क (muṣka, “testicle, scrotum”).

parole.significato: the commander of a cavalry regiment
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الْنَائِب (al-nāʔib, “the representative”).

parole.significato: alqueire, Portuguese bushel, a traditional unit of dry measure equal to 13.1–19.3 liters in different 19th-century cont…
parole.testo: From Arabic الكَيْل (al-kayl, “a measure”), from ك ي ل (k y l).

parole.significato: alkermes (desiccated bodies of female Kermes ilicis and Kermes vermilio insects)
parole.testo: PIE word  *kʷŕ̥mis From Arabic الْقِرْمِز (al-qirmiz).
Borrowed from Arabic الْبَيَاض (al-bayāḍ, “white lead”).
From Arabic البَرَا (al-barā, “bill, certificate”).

parole.significato: construction worker (employee working at a construction)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic بَنَّاء (bannāʔ), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Aragonese arbanyil, Asturian and Spanish albañil, Galician albanel, and Leonese arbañil.
Borrowed from Arabic البِرْكَة (al-birka, “pond, tank”). Compare Spanish alberca.

parole.significato: sheriff (title between Moors and Turks equivalent to sharif, attributed to people descended from Muhammad)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الشَّرِيف (aš-šarīf).
Possibly derived from andar, or Arabic الدَاعِم (ad-dāʕim, “supporter”). Compare Spanish andamio.

parole.significato: tapir (large odd-toed ungulate with a long prehensile upper lip of the family Tapiridae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic لَمْتَة (lamta).

parole.significato: said of a horse with white markings on its legs
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic أَرْجَل (ʔarjal), through Andalusian Arabic.
Borrowed from Arabic الْغُلَّ (al-ḡulla, “the necklace, the shackle”).

parole.significato: warehouse (large building where goods are stored)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic المَخْزَن (al-maḵzan), under the influence of arma. Compare Galician armacén, Spanish almacén, English magazine.
Borrowed from Arabic الرَّبَض (ar-rabaḍ, “outskirts, suburb”).
Borrowed from Arabic الرَّعِيَّة (ar-raʕiyya, “the subjects”).
Borrowed from Arabic اَلرَّئِيس (ar-raʔīs, “the chief, the captain”), from رَأْس (raʔs, “head”), from Proto-Semitic *raʔš- (“head”).

parole.significato: arratel, a traditional unit of mass, usually equivalent to 460 g
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الرَطْل (ar-raṭl) via Andalusian Arabic, from Aramaic רִיטְלָא / ܪܺܝܛܠܳܐ (rīṭlā), variant of לִיטְרָא / ܠܺܝܛܪܳܐ (līṭrā), from Ancient Greek λίτρα (lítra, “libra, Roman pound”). Doublet of libra.
From Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”) or أَسَاسِيُّون (ʔasāsiyyūn, “fundamentalist”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese atabaque, borrowed from Arabic طَبَق (ṭabaq), from طَابَق (ṭābaq), borrowed from Middle Persian tʾp̄k', from Proto-Iranian *tāpaka-, from Proto-Indo-European *tep-. Cognate with Spanish tabaque (“wicker basket”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese atalaya, from Arabic الطَلِيعَة (aṭ-ṭalīʕa, “a scout; and a party of scouts”) (plural الطَلَائِع (aṭ-ṭalāʔiʕ)), from the verb طَالَعَ (ṭālaʕa, “to inspect”), from the root ط ل ع (ṭ l ʕ), the same as طَلَعَ (ṭalaʕa, “to watch”).
Borrowed from Arabic التَابُوت (at-tābūt). Compare Spanish ataúd (“coffin”).
From Arabic تَرَقَّى (taraqqā, “to advance”), possibly with the a- prefix.
Borrowed from Arabic اَلتُّنّ (at-tunn, “tuna”) via Andalusian Arabic, from Latin thunnus, from Ancient Greek θύννος (thúnnos).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: until (up to the time of something happening)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese até, ata of uncertain origin. Possibly from Arabic حَتَّى (ḥattā), Latin ad ista (“to this”) or Latin ad tenus (“as far as”) (>"ad tenes"), which explain the large number of mediaeval variants (atrõe, atée, atrõo, attaa, atẽe, atães, tẽe and so on). However, co
From Arabic أَوْج (ʔawj), from Persian اوگ (owg).

parole.significato: assegai (slim African spear or javelin with an iron tip)
parole.testo: From colloquial Arabic اَلزَّغَايَة (az-zaḡāya), from Proto-Berber *zaġāya (“spear”).

parole.significato: wild olive tree (Olea europaea subsp. europaea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الزَّبُّوج (az-zabbūj).
From Arabic الزَهْر (az-zahr, “the dice”). Compare Spanish azar, Italian zara and French hasard.

parole.significato: to jinx (to bring bad luck to)
parole.testo: From Arabic زَهْر (zahr, “dice”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azeitona, borrowed from Arabic زَيْتُونَة (zaytūna). Compare Asturian and Spanish aceituna.

parole.significato: water mill with a vertical water wheel
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic سَانِيَة (sāniya). Cognate with Galician acea and Spanish aceña.

parole.significato: twitch (object used to hold the snout of animals)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الزِّيَار (az-ziyār).

parole.significato: a narrow footpath lined with fences, walls or hedges, often between villages
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الزِنَقَة (az-zinaqa).
From Arabic الزِنْجَار (az-zinjār, “copper oxide”).

parole.significato: souq (a street market in Arab-speaking countries)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic سُوق (sūq). Doublet of soco and açougue.

parole.significato: scourge (a whip or lash used to inflict severe corporal punishment or self-mortification).
parole.testo: From Arabic سريقة (surriyaqah). Cognate with Spanish zurriaga and Spanish zurriago.
Borrowed from Arabic الزَحْمَة (az-zaḥma, “pressing, thronging”).
Alteration of azémela/azêmela. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese azemela, from Arabic الزَّمِيلَة (az-zamīla, “colleague”).
From Arabic صِقَال (ṣiqāl), from صَقَلَ (ṣaqala). Cognate with Spanish acicalar.

parole.significato: wicker basket (small basket made of thin wicker, with a low edge and oval or round shape, without lid and without handl…
parole.testo: From Arabic سَفَط (safaṭ, “basket”). Compare Spanish azafate.
From earlier açoute. Borrowed from Arabic السَّوْط (as-sawṭ, “the whip”). Compare Galician azoute, Spanish azote, Sicilian zotta and Maltese sawt.

parole.significato: a typical Portuguese dish originating from the southern region of Alentejo, composed of thinly sliced bread with garlic…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الثُرْدَة (aṯ-ṯurda, “tharid”) (see Wikipedia's article on tharid).

From Arabic اَلسُّوق (as-sūq, “the market, the souq”), from Aramaic שוקא or ܫܘܩܐ (šūqā’, “street, market”), from Akkadian 𒋻 (sūqu, “street”), from 𒊓𒀀𒆪 (sāqu, “narrow”). Cognate with Galician azougue, Spanish zoco and Maltese suq. Doublet of soco and azoque.

parole.significato: dam (structure built across a body of water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic السُّدّ (as-sudd, “dam, dike”). Compare Spanish azud and Catalan assut.
From Arabic بِطَانَة (biṭāna, “inside, lining, liner”). Compare Spanish badana.
From Old Galician-Portuguese bairro, barrio, from Arabic بَرِيّ (bariyy, “savage”), referring to the outer, surrounding or less civilized or urbanized parts of a city. Compare Spanish barrio.

parole.significato: to make useless; to cause to fail
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic بَاطِل (bāṭil, “invalid; null; futile”).
Uncertain. Suggested derivations include: * baldo (“lacking”), from Arabic; * Vulgar Latin *batulu for batillum; * Late Latin baiula, feminine of Classical Latin bāiulus (“carriers”).
From Arabic بَنِيَان (baniyān), from Gujarati વાણિયો (vāṇiyo), ultimately from Sanskrit वाणिज (vāṇijá), variant of वणिज् (vaṇíj, “merchant, trader”).

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese baraço /baraça (“rope”), from Arabic مَرَسَة (marasa, “rope”), from Classical Syriac ܡܰܪܫܳܐ (maršā, “rope”), from Akkadian 𒄙 (markasu, “rope”), from Akkadian 𒆟 (rakāsu, “to tie”).
Borrowed from Arabic إِبْلِيس (ʔiblīs, “Iblees, devil”).

parole.significato: Berber (member of northwest African ethnic group)
parole.testo: From Arabic بَرْبَرِيّ (barbariyy, “Berber”), probably from Ancient Greek βᾰ́ρβᾰρος (bắrbăros, “foreign”). Doublet of bárbaro and, possibly, of bravo /brabo.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese berengenha, borrowed from Arabic بَاذِنْجَان (bāḏinjān), borrowed from Classical Persian بَاذِنْگَان (bāzingān), borrowed from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (vātiṅgaṇa), from Proto-Dravidian *waẓVtV. Compare Galician berenxena and Spanish berenjena.

parole.significato: slingshot (Y-shaped device used to shoot projectiles)
parole.testo: From Arabic بُنْدُق (“hazelnuts, small projectiles”).
From Arabic بَلُّوطَة (ballūṭa), perhaps from Ancient Greek βαλανωτή (balanōtḗ), "acorn shaped". Compare Galician belota and Spanish bellota.

parole.significato: bladder wrack (Fucus vesiculosus, an edible seaweed of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic أَبُو طِيلُون (ʔabū ṭīlūn). Doublet of abutilão and abutilo (“abutilon”).
Unknown. Possibly from Arabic قِلَّة البَارَك (qilla(t) al-bārak, “bad luck”).

parole.significato: amount corresponding to the quota that partners pay to enter a game
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic قَفِيز (qafīz).
From Old Galician-Portuguese cafiz, from Arabic قَفِيز (qafīz).
From Arabic كَافِر (kāfir, “infidel”). Attested since 1516 (Dicionário Houaiss da Língua Portuguesa).
From Arabic كفتة (kufta), from Persian کوفته (kufte, “ground meat”).

parole.significato: a type of oil lamp with a restricted (jar or pitcher-like) shape and a wick spout on one of its sides
parole.testo: From Arabic قِنْدِيل (qindīl). Cognate with Galician and Spanish candil and Turkish kandil.

From Arabic قِرْطَاس (qirṭās), from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “sheet of paper”), from χαράσσω (kharássō, “to scratch, to inscribe”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰer- (“to scratch”). Cognate to English chart. Doublet of carta.

parole.significato: casbah (the fortress in a city in North Africa or the Middle East)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic قَصَبَة (qaṣaba). Doublet of alcáçova.
Borrowed from Arabic صَيْف (ṣayf, “summer”). Cognate with Galician ceifa (“harvesting”).
Borrowed from Arabic سِرْوَال (sirwāl, “pants”).

parole.significato: satin (cloth with a glossy surface and a dull back)
parole.testo: From Arabic السَاتَان زَيْتُون (as-sātān zaytūn, “satin from Zaitun”), a city in China, perhaps 新疆 (Xīnjiāng), a port during the middle ages.
From Arabic صِهْرِيج (ṣihrīj), from Middle Persian. Compare Galician chafariz, Spanish jaraíz (“vat”) and Catalan safareig (“artificial water deposit”).
Borrowed from Arabic شَهَادَة (šahāda).
Borrowed from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā, “caraway”), via Andalusian Arabic.
Borrowed from Arabic كُرْكُم (kurkum, “turmeric”).

parole.significato: couscous (semolina-based pasta of North African origin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese cozcuz, borrowed from Arabic كُسْكُس (kuskus). Compare Spanish cuscús and French couscous.
Borrowed from Arabic قَاضٍ (qāḍin). Doublet of alicali.
From Arabic قَافِلَة (qāfila).

parole.significato: dinar (name of official currency of several countries)
parole.testo: From Arabic دِينَار (dīnār, “dinar”), from Aramaic דֵּינָרָא / ܕܝܢܪܐ (dēnārā), from Ancient Greek δηνάριον (dēnárion), from Latin dēnārius. Doublet of dinheiro and denário.
Borrowed from Arabic علج (ʿilj).
Possibly from Arabic, or a pronunciation of an indigenous name for the bird.

parole.significato: of hair, ropes, cables and similar, to tangle; to snarl (to interweave in a messy way)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese embaraçar, from Arabic مَرَسَة (marasa, “rope”). Cognate with Spanish embarazar and English embarrass. By surface analysis, en- + baraço + -ar or embaraço + -ar.

parole.significato: layette (collection of clothes and objects necessary for the service and use of a baby or a person who is going to or i…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الشَّوَار (aš-šawār, “wedding gift”).
From Arabic إِسْفَانَاخ (ʔisfānāḵ), from Persian اسپناخ (espanâx). Compare Spanish espinaca.
Borrowed from Arabic فَجْر (fajr, “dawn”).

parole.significato: felucca (type of boat used to transport passengers and goods across the river Tagus)
parole.testo: From Arabic فَلُوكَة (falūka).
From faianca (“crude object”) + -aria, from Arabic فَنْقَة (fanqa, “sack”).

parole.significato: faqir (a religious mendicant who owns no personal property)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic فَقِير (faqīr, “poor man”).
Borrowed from Arabic فَرْدَة (farda, “cloth, woman's clothes”). Cognate with fardo.
Probably from Arabic فَرْد (fard, “one of a pair”), as applied to saddlebags. Alternative theories include Arabic فَرْض (farḍ, “crease”) and Latin fartus (“filled”). See Spanish fardo for more.

parole.significato: carousal (noisy feast or social gathering, especially one with alcohol)
parole.testo: Uncertain origin. Possible origins include: * from dialectal Arabic فَرْحَة (farḥa); * from Latin pānis farreus (“spelt bread”); * from fanfarra (“fanfare”).
Borrowed from Arabic فُتَات (futāt, “crumbs, pieces”).
Unknown, but likely ultimately from Arabic.
Borrowed from Arabic حُرّ (ḥurr, “free”). Cognate with Spanish horro and Swahili huru.
Borrowed from Arabic فُلَان (fulān). Doublet of fulano.

parole.significato: fatwa (legal opinion issued by a mufti)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic فَتْوَى (fatwā).
From Arabic غُرْفَة (ḡurfa); see carafe for more.

parole.significato: jerboa (any of several small rodent of the family Dipodidae)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Arabic جَرْبُوع (jarbūʕ) or يَرْبُوع (yarbūʕ).

parole.significato: sesame (Sesamum indicum, a plant cultivated for seeds)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Arabic جُلْجُلَان (juljulān, “sesame”) via a dialect. Sicilian giurgiulena.
Alteration of ginete, from Arabic زَنَاتِيّ (zanātiyy).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese genete, from Arabic زَنَاتِيّ (zanātiyy), via Andalusian Arabic, the Zenati or Zenata Berbers, known as excellent horse breeders.

parole.significato: chalk (a piece of chalk used for drawing and on a blackboard)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic جِبْس (jibs, “gypsum”), from Latin gypsum (“plaster”), from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos). Doublet of gesso, which was inherited.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese guitarra, borrowed from Arabic قِيثَارَة (qīṯāra), borrowed from Aramaic קיתרא (qīṯārā), borrowed from Ancient Greek κῐθᾰ́ρᾱ (kĭthắrā), from Pre-Greek. Doublet of cítara, cítola, and cistre.
Borrowed from Arabic حَجِّي (ḥajjī).

parole.significato: halal (allowable, according to Muslim religious customs)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic حَلَال (ḥalāl).
Borrowed from Arabic حَرَام (ḥarām). Doublet of harém.

parole.significato: hashish (dried leaves of the Indian hemp plant used as a narcotic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic حَشِيش (ḥašīš, “hay, dried herb”).
Ultimately from Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ). Doublet of henê.

parole.significato: hadith (collected sayings and actions of Muhammad)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic حَدِيث (ḥadīṯ).
Borrowed from Arabic عِيد (ʕīd).
From Arabic إِمَام (ʔimām).
Borrowed from Arabic اِنْتِفَاضَة (intifāḍa, “shaking off, uprising, insurrection”).
Borrowed from Arabic جَهَاز (jahāz, “equipment”).

parole.significato: jug; ewer; pitcher (deep vessel for holding liquids)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic جَرَّة (jarra).

Borrowed from Arabic خِنْزِير جَبَلِيّ (ḵinzīr jabaliyy, literally “pig of the mountains”) via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Galician xabaril, xabarín, Asturian xabalín, Spanish jabalí (whence English javelina) and Aragonese chabalin.
Unadapted borrowing from Arabic جِهَاد (jihād, “struggle; effort”).
Borrowed from Arabic جُنْك (junk).

parole.significato: centipede (segmented arthropod of class Chilopoda), especially one that is venomous
parole.testo: Ultimately from Arabic العَقْرَب (al-ʕaqrab, “scorpion”). Doublet of lacrau.
From Old Galician-Portuguese alacran (“scorpion”), from Arabic العَقْرَب (al-ʕaqrab, “scorpion”). Doublet of lacraia. Compare Spanish alacrán.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese laranja, from Arabic نَارَنْج (nāranj), from Persian نارنگ (nârang), from Sanskrit नारङ्ग (nāraṅga, “orange tree”), itself of uncertain origin, possibly Dravidian. Compare Spanish naranja.
Borrowed from Arabic إِعْلَام (ʔiʕlām).
From Old Galician-Portuguese lezira, from Arabic جَزِيرَة (jazīra, “island”).

parole.significato: slowworm (Anguis fragilis, a legless Old-World lizard)
parole.testo: From Arabic عَقْرَب (ʕaqrab, “scorpion”), compare lacrau.
From Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn, “lemon, lime”).
Borrowed from Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn) via Andalusian Arabic, from Persian لیمون /لیمو (limun, limu), from Sanskrit निम्बू (nimbū).

Uncertain. Possibly from massa (“dough”) + -io. Or, from Arabic ماسي (masi). Also compare Italian and Latin malacia, from Ancient Greek μαλακός (malakós, “soft”). Cognates with Proto-Slavic *mękъkъ (“soft”).

parole.significato: madrasa (a school that teaches Islamic theology)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic مَدْرَسَة (madrasa, “school”).

parole.significato: a large sculpture representing a person
parole.testo: From the proper name Mafoma, form of Arabic مُحَمَّد (muḥammad).

parole.significato: mameluke (member of a military regime in mediaeval and early modern Egypt and Syria)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic مَمْلُوك (mamlūk, “slave”).
Borrowed from Arabic مَرْأَة هَيْنَة (marʔa hayna, literally “deceiving woman”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese almafi, from Arabic عَظْم اَلْفِيل (ʕaẓm al-fīl, “elephant-bone”), from عَظْم (ʕaẓm, “bone”) + فِيل (fīl, “elephant”). Compare Galician, Spanish, and Catalan marfil.
Borrowed from Arabic مُحَرَّم (muḥarram, “forbidden”). Doublet of marrano, from Spanish marrano.
Borrowed from Arabic مَطْمُورَة (maṭmūra).
Borrowed from Arabic مَطْرَق (maṭraq, “stick, hammer”). See Aramaic מטרקא (mṭrqʾ) for more.
From matulo + -ão, from Arabic.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Alteration of balancia (“watermelon”), of uncertain origin, possibly from Arabic بَلَنْسِيّ (balansiyy, “Valencian”); influenced by melão (“melon”). First attested in 1587. Noun 2 sense 1 and adjective sense 1 are in reference to the appearance of watermelons, being green on the exterior and red (as
Borrowed from Arabic مِسْكِين (miskīn, “poor”). Compare Galician mesquiño, Spanish mezquino, French mesquin.

parole.significato: mosque (a place of worship for Muslims)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese mesquita, mezquita (“mosque”), from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid), from the verb سَجَدَ (sajada, “to bow down”), from the root س ج د (s j d).
Borrowed from Arabic مِثْقَال (miṯqāl, “weight”).

parole.significato: mocha (a type of strong Arabian coffee)
parole.testo: From Mocha, Yemen, a port on the Red Sea, from Arabic اَلْمُخَا (al-muḵā), a major marketplace for coffee during Ottoman rule.
Borrowed from Arabic مَوْسِم (mawsim).
Borrowed from Arabic مُسْتَعْرَب (mustaʕrab, “Arabized”).
From Arabic مُفْتٍ (muftin), the active participle of أَفْتَى (ʔaftā, “to deliver a formal opinion”).
Borrowed from Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim).
Borrowed from classical Arabic مُومِيَاء (mūmiyāʔ), from Persian مومیا (mumyâ), from موم (mum, “wax”).

parole.significato: noria (waterwheel with buckets, used to raise water)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic نَاعُورَة (nāʕūra), from Classical Syriac ܢܥܘܪܬܐ (nāʿōrtāʾ, “water wheel; growler”). Cognate with Spanish noria.

parole.significato: a place-name prefix found in some river names and place names
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic وَادٍ (wādin, “river”). Doublet of Guade-.

parole.significato: gecko (any lizard of the family Gekkonidae)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic وَزَغَة (wazaḡa).
Borrowed from Arabic أبو طاقة (’abū ṭāqa)
From Arabic بَطِيخَة (baṭīḵa, “watermelon”).

parole.significato: duck (any aquatic bird of the family Anatidae)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pato (“duck”), from Andalusian Arabic بَطّ (paṭṭ), from Arabic بَطّ (baṭṭ, “duck”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish pato and Swahili bata.

parole.parola: que a paz esteja com ele
parole.testo: Calque of Arabic عَلَيْهِ ٱلسَّلَامُ (ʕalayhi s-salāmu). Literally, “may the peace be with him”.
From Arabic كِبَّة (kibba, “ball”) and كُبَّة (kubba, “ball”).

parole.significato: metric carat (unit of mass for precious stones and pearls, equal to 200 mg)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic قِيرَاط (qīrāṭ), from Ancient Greek κεράτιον (kerátion). Cognate with Galician and Spanish quilate.

From Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā), or from Latin chimicus, alternative form of chēmicus (“chemical”), from chēmia (“chemistry”), Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”).
With variant arrebite, from Arabic رَبِط (rabiṭ).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese arrafẽes, borrowed from Arabic رَهِين (rahīn). Cognate with Galician refén and Spanish rehén.

parole.significato: a pastry of fine flour, kolach
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese regueifa, from Andalusian Arabic [Term?], from Arabic رَغِيفَة (raḡīfa, “loaf”), colloquial variant of رَغِيف (raḡīf, “loaf”). Cognate with Galician regueifa and Spanish regaifa.

parole.significato: ream (set of twenty hands of paper or five hundred sheets)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic رِزْمَة (rizma). Compare Catalan raima and Spanish resma.
Borrowed from Arabic رَتَم (ratam).
Borrowed from Arabic سَفْرة (safra, “trip, voyage”), because itinerant workers would travel during the harvest season. Cognate with Spanish zafra (“sugar cane harvest”).
Borrowed from Arabic اَلسَّلَامُ عَلَيْك (as-salāmu ʕalayk, “peace be upon you”).

Borrowed from Arabic سَلَاوِيّ (salāwiyy), the nisba of سَلَا (salā, “Salé”), a city regarded from al-Andalus as markedly Berber, and thus Barbaric. The original Portuguese sense only referred to the rural region around Lisbon.
Borrowed from Arabic صَنِفَة (ṣanifa, “border of a dress”).
Borrowed from Arabic حَرْذُون (ḥarḏūn). Compare Galician xardón.
Borrowed from Arabic صَرَّف (ṣarraf).

Probably so named because its crest of long feathers resembles quill pens stuck behind the ears of an office clerk; alternatively, possibly from Arabic صَقْر اَلطَّائِر (ṣaqr aṭ-ṭāʔir, “hunter bird”), from صَقْر (ṣaqr, “falcon, hawk”) طَائِر (ṭāʔir, “bird”); see secretary bird.

parole.significato: accent (the manner of speaking or pronouncing peculiar to a community)
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from dialectal Arabic *صَوْتَك (*ṣōtak, “your voice”), corresponding to standard صَوْتُكَ (ṣawtuka). According to the Houaiss Dictionary, first attested in the early 18th century.
From Arabic سُقَاطَة (suqāṭa, “object without value”), see سقط (saqaṭ).
From Old Galician-Portuguese çumo, from Arabic زُوم (zūm, “juice, sap”), from Ancient Greek ζωμός (zōmós). Cognate of Galician zume and Spanish zumo.

parole.significato: sunnah (Muhammad’s way of life, as recorded in the hadiths)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic سُنَّة (sunna, “habit, custom”).

parole.significato: dessert made with milk, eggs and sugar
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic طَبِخ (ṭabiḵ, “cooked (food)”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese taful, tafur, from Arabic تَكْفُور (takfūr, “Armenian king”), from Middle Armenian թագւոր (tʻagwor, “king”), from Old Armenian թագաւոր (tʻagawor, “king”), from Parthian *tag(a)-bar (“king”, literally “crown bearing”). Cognate with Galician tafur, Spanish tahúr, Catalan t
Probably from Arabic تَكَلَّم (takallam, “to talk”).
From Arabic طَحِينَة (ṭaḥīna), from the root ط ح ن (ṭ-ḥ-n) related to grinding. Final -e is the standard pronunciation in Levantine Arabic.

parole.significato: date palm (palm tree whose fruit is the date)
parole.testo: From tâmara (“date”) + -eira, from Arabic.

parole.significato: drum (a type of percussive musical instrument)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese atanbor, from Arabic الطُنْبُور (aṭ-ṭunbūr); cognate to Persian طبل (“drum”), Spanish and Galician tambor.

parole.parola: tapar o sol com a peneira
parole.significato: To try to hide something that is evident.
parole.testo: Literally, “to cover the sun with the sieve”. Perhaps after Arabic غَطَّى الشَّمْسَ بِالْغِرْبالِ (ḡaṭṭā š-šamsa bi-l-ḡirbāli), whence Maltese għatta x-xemx bl-għarbiel.

parole.significato: tare (the empty weight of a container)
parole.testo: From Arabic طَرْحَة (ṭarḥa, “that which is thrown away”). Compare Italian tara and French tare, taré (“crazy”).
Borrowed from Arabic تَرَائِك (tarāʔik), plural of تَرِيكَة (tarīka), via Andalusian Arabic. Cognate with Spanish tareco.
From Vulgar Arabic طَرِيحَة (ṭarīḥa, “endeavor”). Compare tarefa.
Borrowed from Arabic تُرُنْجَة (turunja, “citron”). Compare Spanish toronja (“grapefruit”) and Catalan taronja (“orange”).

parole.significato: lupin (any plant of the genus Lupinus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic تُرْمُس (turmus), from Aramaic תורמוסא / ܬܘܪܡܣܐ (tūrmūsā, “lupine”), from Akkadian 𒋻𒄷 (TAR.MUŠ₈ /⁠tarmuš⁠/), from Sumerian 𒋻𒄷 (TAR.MUŠ₈ /⁠tarmuš⁠/). Also found as Ancient Greek θέρμος (thérmos) and Coptic ⲑⲁⲣⲙⲟⲩⲥ (tharmous) and in the taxonomical Lupinus albus subsp. termis.

Uncertain. Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tripa, possibly from Arabic تَرْب (tarb, “bowels”), or perhaps connected to Old Norse torf (“turf, sod”) (see e.g. Middle Irish tarpán/torpán (“bunch of grapes; clod”)). See Spanish tripa and Italian trippa.

parole.significato: typhoon (weather phenomenon in the Pacific, equivalent to a hurricane)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic طُوفَان (ṭūfān, “storm; typhoon”). See etymology in typhoon.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tamara, from Arabic تَمْرَة (tamra).

parole.significato: waw (name of the Arabic letter و (w))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic وَاو (wāw).
Borrowed from Arabic عُود (ʕūd).
Borrowed from Arabic جِلَال (jilāl).

parole.significato: checkmate (conclusive victory in a game of chess)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَاه مَاتَ (šāh māta). from Persian شاه مات (šâh mât, “the king is ambushed/conquered”).
Borrowed from Arabic شَبُّوطَة (šabbūṭa).

The original meaning of “hairy” semantically extended to refe
Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيط (šarīṭ). Compare Spanish jareta.
Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيعَة (šarīʕa, literally “path, way”).
Borrowed from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”). Compare Spanish jarabe and Catalan xarop.
Borrowed from Arabic شَاوَرْمَا (šāwarmā), شَاوِرْمَا (šāwirmā), from Ottoman Turkish چویرمه (çevirme, “spinning, rotating”).
Ultimately from Arabic شَبَّاك (šabbāk, “fishing boat; small warship”). Compare xávega.
Borrowed from Arabic شَيْخ (šayḵ).

parole.significato: check (when the king is directly threatened by an enemy piece)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَاه (šāh), from Persian شاه (šâh, “king”), from Middle Persian 𐭬𐭫𐭪𐭠 (šāh, “king”), from Old Persian 𐏋 (XŠ /⁠xšāyaθiya⁠/, “king”), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ksayati (“he rules, he has power over”), from Proto-Indo-European *tke- (“to gain power over, gain control over”). Doublet

parole.significato: checkmate (conclusive victory in a game of chess)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَاه مَاتَ (šāh māta). from Persian شاه مات (šâh mât, “the king is ambushed/conquered”).

parole.significato: sharif (title used by Moorish princes who claimed to be descendants of Muhammad)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيف (šarīf, “noble”). Compare Spanish jerife.

parole.significato: Shiite (of, or relating to Shiites or the Shi'a branch of Islam)
parole.testo: From Arabic شِيعَة (šīʕa, “Shia”) + -ita.

parole.significato: a form of artisanal fishing which involves setting nets in the sea and then trawling them using animals or machines in…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَبَكَة (šabaka, “net”). Compare Spanish jábega.

parole.significato: wild olive tree (Olea europaea subsp. europaea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic الزَّبُّوج (az-zabbūj).
Borrowed from Arabic زَرْبَطَانَة (zarbaṭāna, “blowgun”).
Borrowed from Arabic زَانِيَة.
Borrowed from Arabic سُرِّيَة (surriya, “concubine”).

parole.significato: zenith (point vertically above a position or observer)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”).
From Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”), via Spanish or Medieval Latin.
From Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr), through Latin algebra.
Unknown, perhaps from Malay buli, buli-buli (“small stoppered vial or flask of glass or porcelain”), or from Arabic بُلْبُلَة (bulbula).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese dado, itself from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, of uncertain origin; possibly from Classical Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”), or from Latin datum. Compare Spanish dado, Catalan dau, Italian dado, French dé.
Uncertain. Maybe from Spanish jineta or from Arabic.

From Paleo-Hispanic (compare Basque sasi, earlier çarzi). Alternatively, from Arabic شَرَا (šarā, “plant with thorns”), from سَارَاسَا (sārāsā, “to be evil, vicious”). Cognate with Asturian, Spanish, and Ladino zarza.
